10.1002_adma.72926: 2D Silver Nanosheet Assembly for Nanomembranes Partially overlapped silver nanosheets form robust face-to-face junctions that remain electrically connected during stretching, preserving conductive pathways. This controlled 2D assembly enables an ultrathin, isotropically stretchable nanomembrane with exceptional conductivity and mechanical robustness. More details can be found in the Research Article by Qingchang Liu, Dae-Hyeong Kim, Tae-Wook Kim, and co-workers (DOI: 10.1002/adma.202516002).
10.1002_advs.77650: The surface modification of zinc anodes and the development of effective cathode dual‐functional oxygen electrocatalysts remain of paramount interest for enhancing the cycle life of rechargeable zinc‐air batteries. The present work provides a sustainable synthesis of CoNi‐based composites that can be used as cathode and anode side catalysts in Zn‐air batteries. CoNi‐metals with hybrid‐metal organic frameworks (Hybrid‐MOFs) and MOF‐derived composites from curcumin‐melamine (C‐M) and benzene‐1,3,5‐tricarboxylic acid (BTC) were created for cathode and anode composites using reflux and hydrothermal techniques. In this instance, the cathode composite can be referred to as CoNi‐N‐C after annealing, whereas the anode composite can be referred to as CoNi‐BTC without annealing. Thereafter, the formation of CoNi‐N‐C and CoNi‐BTC composites was confirmed by microscopic, X‐ray photoelectron, and X‐ray diffraction techniques. As a result, structurally tailored CoNi‐N‐C and CoNi‐BTC composites perform efficiently in electrochemical processes such as oxygen evolution/reduction reactions (OER/ORR) and energy conversion devices (Zn‐air battery). Primarily, the CoNi‐N‐C catalyst exhibits the lowest overpotential (E i = 10 = 1.48 V) and better half‐wave potential (E 1/2 = 0.781 V) in OER/ORR reactions; secondary CoNi‐BTC composites coated on the Zn anode have the highest specific capacity (756.3 mA h g zn −1 ) and 1000‐cycle charge–discharge stability in Zn‐air batteries.
10.1016_j.ijhydene.2026.156547: A unified electro-thermal modeling framework is indispensable for prudently coordinating multi-energy flows with waste heat recovery and reuse in fuel cell heavy-duty trucks (FCHDT), thereby improving hydrogen utilization behavior. During the operation, the rise in fuel cell stack temperature creates a heating energy mismatch with the sharply increased demand of the cabin and container under low temperature conditions, thereby deteriorating the overall operating efficiency of FCHDT. To overcome this limitation, we develop a system-level electro–thermal coupled modeling framework for FCHDT with thermal demand and heat supply interactions. Building on the classical electrical load model, a multi-zone thermal load model of FCHDT is developed to capture the coupled energy demands under prescribed driving and environmental conditions. Herein, the thermal loads of the cabin and container are explicitly modeled to utilize the surplus waste heat from the fuel cell system, while any unmet thermal demand is converted into equivalent electrical loads supplied by the HVAC system. On the supply side, physics models of the fuel cell system and battery are developed, with fuel cell operation influenced by heat generation and cooling capacity limits. Furthermore, the proposed electro–thermal balance model enables a physical representation of the appropriate match for power supply and demand interactions. Simulation showcase that explicitly accounting for electro–thermal coupling shows approximately 9.7% lower hydrogen consumption, thereby underscoring the influence of system-level modeling with heating coordination in advancing the energy efficiency and operational robustness of FCHDT. © 2026 Published by Elsevier Ltd. 10.1016_j.ijhydene.2026.156806: Decarbonising data centres requires energy systems that reconcile electricity demand with variable renewable generation. We develop an hourly techno-economic framework integrating stochastic IT demand, climate-dependent power usage effectiveness, photovoltaic generation, workload flexibility, and storage pathways based on battery energy storage systems (BESS) or green hydrogen for a 10 MW IT facility in Phoenix, Frankfurt, and Singapore. A genetic algorithm sizes the systems, hourly rule-based dispatch evaluates operation, and costs are annualised over a 25-year lifetime subject to a minimum 80% renewable fraction. BESS achieves lower levelised cost of electricity (0.097–0.206 USD/kWh) than hydrogen (0.155–0.295 USD/kWh) because of higher round-trip efficiency and lower conversion-related capital requirements. Terminal-state-constrained repeated-seed optimisation preserves this ranking, while combined BESS–hydrogen searches return battery-only designs at the target. Sensitivity analysis identifies photovoltaic and storage capital costs, grid electricity price, discount rate, conversion efficiency, and climate-sensitive demand as the dominant economic drivers.
